entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Pharmacy, the science and practice of preparing, dispensing, and reviewing medications, emerged from humanity's earliest attempts to treat illness and alleviate suffering, with its roots stretching back over 70,000 years to prehistoric use of medicinal plants. Its development is inextricably linked to the evolution of medicine, chemistry, and botany, providing the fundamental means by which therapeutic agents are made accessible. From ancient Mesopotamian clay tablets detailing remedies to the sophisticated pharmaceutical laboratories of the Classical and post-Classical eras, pharmacy has continuously adapted, professionalized, and expanded its scope, profoundly shaping human health and longevity across every civilization.

The formalization of pharmacy began in antiquity, with Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BCE) documenting over 700 drugs and their preparations in ancient Egypt, and Sumerian cuneiform tablets from 2100 BCE describing medicinal recipes. The Greek physician Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BCE) emphasized rational observation, while Dioscorides's *De Materia Medica* (1st century CE) cataloged over 600 medicinal plants, becoming a foundational text for 1,500 years. During the Islamic Golden Age (8th–13th centuries), pharmacy experienced its most significant advancements; Baghdad saw the establishment of the first dedicated pharmacies (saydaliyah) in the 8th century, separating the roles of physician and pharmacist. Scholars like al-Razi (Rhazes, 865–925 CE) and Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980–1037 CE) meticulously documented drug preparation, classification, and pharmacology, introducing precise weights, measures, and new dosage forms such as syrups and ointments.
